extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political theory, comparative government, and 19th-century American studies
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical chapter describing the principal causes that sustain a democratic republic (with a focus on the United States), examining institutional, social, religious, and economic factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal form of Government
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal form of Government which the Americans have adopted, and which enables the Union to combine the power of a great empire with the security of a small State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as one of the three principal causes maintaining the democratic republic: a federal constitution balances large-scale power with local security and thereby helps sustain republican institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Municipal institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Those municipal institutions which limit the despotism of the majority, and at the same time impart a taste for freedom and a knowledge of the art of being free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local/self-government is credited with curbing majority tyranny and educating citizens in practical freedom; municipal life imparts habits and know-how necessary for republican stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitution of the judicial power
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution of the judicial power: courts of justice serve to repress the excesses of democracy, and to check and direct the impulses of the majority without stopping its activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judiciary plays a balancing role—restraining democratic excesses while allowing majority action to continue; courts are a key institutional brake on popular impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manners (mores) as a political cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Manners (used in the ancient sense of mores) meaning the whole moral and intellectual condition of a people—various notions and opinions current among men—which contribute to the maintenance of political institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes simple tastes, orderly manners, domestic affections, and attachments (or lack thereof) to birthplace; these social habits influence political stability by shaping civic behavior and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion as a direct political institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion (Christianity broadly) operates as a political institution: 'North America peopled by men who professed a democratic and republican Christianity' and religion is viewed as powerfully contributing to maintenance of the democratic republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that the sects brought to America tended to a democratic form of Christianity which allied with politics to sustain republicanism; the Catholic population, under separation of church and state, is argued to be especially disposed to equality and republican politics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catholicism's social/political effect under separation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the priesthood is separated from government (as in the United States), Catholics tend to adopt democratic and republican political principles because their social position (often poor and minority) incentivizes support for rights open to all citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why Catholicism—contrary to common assumption—can be compatible with and supportive of equality and republicanism in the American context; includes explanation of clerical role dividing revealed doctrine from political inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion's indirect influence via morals and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Religion indirectly maintains the republic by directing manners: Christian morality shared across sects regulates domestic life, respects marriage, restrains imagination and rash innovation, and thus provides moral limits that stabilize free institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: religion fosters austerity of manners, protects conjugal ties, and women as protectors of morals; religiously-instilled restraints check revolutionary impulses and render political experiments less likely to become destructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abundance of land and continuous emigration (physical/economic causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical causes: the United States offered an 'empty continent' with inexhaustible natural resources; continuous emigration and available land promoted prosperity, mobility, and prevented over-division of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed features: North America was largely uninhabited agricultural land; Americans and new immigrants moved westward continually; this double emigration (Europe→coast and Americans→interior) kept labor in demand and prevented scarcity-induced unrest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws and circumstances limiting excessive division of property
rubrics_metrics.description: Although laws (e.g., abolition of primogeniture) favor division of property, practical circumstances (abundance of land and emigration) prevent property from being divided to excess and thereby avert social evils tied to extreme parceling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited evidence: Massachusetts and New England practices—eldest son taking the land in practice, small estates rarely subdivided further; legislative abolition of primogeniture but social/economic dynamics re-establish similar outcomes without injustice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial passions and practical habits over theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans' dominant passions are commercial rather than political; they introduce business habits into politics, favor order, regular conduct, good sense that amasses fortunes, and hold practice in higher esteem than theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These commercial/practical dispositions encourage orderly public life and temper abstract radicalism; preference for positive calculation over grand general ideas helps maintain political stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social mobility, restlessness for improvement, and its political effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A restless desire for riches and constant emigration—people leaving birthplaces to seek fortune—produce social mobility and ambition that both foster prosperity and limit entrenched social hierarchies, with mixed effects on happiness and permanence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations include rapid interior settlement, ephemeral habitations (deserted dwellings left behind), and the idea that prosperity changes opinions and tempers prior radicalism; this mobility is both a stabilizer (promotes equality of opportunity) and a source of inconstancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusion of knowledge and its favorable role
rubrics_metrics.description: In America, 'too much knowledge cannot be diffused'—widespread knowledge benefits both possessors and the unpossessed and does not produce dangerous new wants; diffusion of knowledge supports prosperity and civil order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as a positive: broad dissemination of knowledge is not feared because it can be satisfied and channels passions into legitimate objects, aiding the use of free institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion regarded as indispensable to republican institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans commonly hold that religious belief is indispensable to the maintenance of republican institutions; religion is widely accepted as facilitating use of liberty even if private conviction varies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supports the broader argument that public deference to religion (even if partly habitual or performative) provides communal moral anchors that buttress civic order—illustrated by anecdote of a court rejecting an atheist witness for undermining trust.
